headline: New Jersey nuclear task force maps next steps for 1,100-megawatt expansion
dek: The group’s first meeting created five subcommittees and a public information hub as New Jersey moves from lifting its nuclear moratorium toward planning new generation.
body: New Jersey’s newly formed Nuclear Task Force held its first meeting Thursday, beginning a state effort to determine how next-generation nuclear power could fit into the state’s future electricity system. Governor Mikie Sherrill’s office said the group reviewed a draft charter, created five subcommittees and launched Nuclear NJ, a public website for updates and background information.

The meeting marks a shift from changing state policy to working out the practical questions that would come before a new reactor could be built. The administration says the task force is intended to coordinate work across government and with industry, labor, environmental groups and other stakeholders. It is not itself an approval for a plant, and the governor’s announcement did not identify a project site, developer or construction schedule.

The five subcommittees divide that work into the areas most likely to shape any future proposal. One will examine regulatory and permitting requirements. Others will study financing and power-sale arrangements, supply chains and technology, workforce development, and public trust. The last category is especially consequential for a technology that requires long-term safety oversight and community participation before construction could move forward.

The task force has 14 members, according to its public roster. The group includes leaders from the governor’s office, the Board of Public Utilities, the Department of Environmental Protection, the Economic Development Authority, the state treasurer’s office and the Department of Military Affairs. It also includes representatives of PSEG Nuclear, Holtec, the New Jersey Business and Industry Association, electrical workers, the Laborers’ International Union of North America and the Natural Resources Defense Council. That mix gives the panel access to industry and labor expertise, while also putting potential environmental and public-interest concerns inside the same planning process.

The new group follows two major policy steps. Sherrill’s Executive Order 2 established a nuclear power task force on her first day in office. In April, she signed legislation that ended New Jersey’s roughly 50-year de facto moratorium on new nuclear development. The state later enacted the Power NJ Act, which directs a competitive procurement program designed to support at least 1,100 megawatts of advanced nuclear generation. The bill describes that number as a program design parameter, not a guarantee that the state will ultimately buy that amount of power.

New Jersey already relies heavily on nuclear generation. The governor’s office says existing nuclear plants provide more than 40% of the state’s electricity and about 80% of its carbon-free power. Supporters frame new reactors as a way to add reliable supply as electricity demand grows and to put downward pressure on utility costs. Those are policy goals, not results that have been demonstrated by a new project; any cost, schedule, waste, safety and siting questions would have to be resolved through later regulatory and procurement decisions.

Independent reporting by New Jersey 101.5 described Thursday’s meeting as the start of planning for the 1,100-megawatt program and noted that the work is focused on permits, financing, workforce needs and public support. That account also underscored the distance between a planning target and operating power: the task force can organize the state’s next steps, but it cannot by itself make a reactor economical, secure federal approvals or settle questions about who bears construction risk.

For residents, the immediate development is therefore an information and planning structure rather than a construction announcement. Nuclear NJ, developed with the Board of Public Utilities, the Economic Development Authority and the Department of Environmental Protection, is intended to collect agency updates and explain the state’s approach. The next meaningful tests will be whether the subcommittees publish clear work products, how the state handles public input and whether any future procurement produces a proposal that can pass technical, financial, environmental and safety review. Sources: [New Jersey Governor’s Office](https://www.nj.gov/governor/news/2026/20261001b.shtml), [New Jersey Nuclear Task Force roster](https://www.nj.gov/nuclear/about/task-force/), [New Jersey Department of Environmental Protection energy policy page](https://dep.nj.gov/cleanenergy/nj/), [New Jersey 101.5 reporting](https://nj1015.com/new-jersey-nuclear-task-force-launches/), and [Nuclear NJ information hub](https://www.nj.gov/nuclear/).
